plants.truth: Blackstone (Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book IV, ch. 2) says the opposite. He reports that Grotius, Pufendorf and other foreign jurists allow necessity to excuse stealing food, calls this 'an unwarranted doctrine, borrowed from the notions of some civilians', and says the law of England admits no such excuse, because English law provides for the poor and the Crown can pardon. Read's picture (a law that formally condemns the starving thief, mitigated by judges and juries) fits Blackstone; the inference that the law 'was never against' the thief rests on the misattribution. Checked against the Avalon Project text of Book IV, ch. 2.

plants.truth: Read's Inquiry (1829) is, by its title and purpose, a defence of the natural grounds of the right to vendible property. Within that project a right of the poor to support works as a condition of the legitimacy and security of property, a line closer to Hume and Paley's prudential case for poor relief than to Paine or Spence. The passage's limiting clause ('with as little hurt as he can to his more fortunate brethren') and its stress that the right covers only 'the sustenance immediately necessary' support reading it as a bounded necessity right and an argument for a legal poor provision, not a call to resistance. Defensible, though less often given than the radical reading.
